title: Sezary Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Sezary syndrome is a rare and aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, often presenting as generalized erythroderma with associated lymphadenopathy, pruritus, and circulating atypical lymphocytes (Sezary cells). This condition may arise spontaneously or evolve from mycosis fungoides. Due to its overlapping features with benign skin disorders, Sezary syndrome poses a diagnostic challenge for clinicians. The disease is characterized by diffuse erythematous plaques or patches, requiring a skin biopsy, lymph node biopsy, and peripheral smear for accurate diagnosis. Early detection and intervention are critical to improving patient outcomes and mitigating the disease's progression and systemic impact.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity enhances the learner’s competence in recognizing and diagnosing Sezary syndrome through detailed clinical evaluations and appropriate diagnostic measures such as biopsies and peripheral smears. Participants develop an understanding of the nuanced differences between Sezary syndrome and mycosis fungoides. Collaborating within an interprofessional team, including dermatologists, pathologists, and oncologists, ensures comprehensive care, leading to accurate diagnoses, timely interventions, and improved patient outcomes. By focusing on evidence-based diagnostic and management strategies, this course equips healthcare professionals with the tools to optimize care for patients with this rare malignancy.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate Sezary syndrome from other forms of cutaneous T-cell lymphomas and benign skin conditions. Screen for diagnostic markers such as circulating Sezary cells, CD4:CD8 ratio abnormalities, and molecular markers. Implement appropriate skin biopsy techniques and lymph node evaluation for accurate diagnosis. Coordinate strategies among interprofessional team members to educate patients on managing their severe pruritis and prescribe medications to relieve the itch, which will enhance the delivery of care for those with Sezary syndrome. title: Sezary Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Sezary syndrome and mycosis fungoides are the most common forms of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) and can mimic benign skin disorders, which can be a diagnostic challenge to clinicians. Though mycosis fungoides is the most common cutaneous lymphoma, it constitutes less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphoma cases. Researchers hypothesize that Sezary syndrome can evolve gradually from mycosis fungoides or occur spontaneously. Significant evidence has been established that Sezary syndrome and mycosis fungoides are closely related and constitute the broad spectrum of cutaneous lymphomas. [1] [2] [3]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Primary cutaneous lymphomas (PCL) are localized to the skin without extracutaneous involvement at the initial diagnosis and are a subset of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. They can originate from T or B lymphocytes called cutaneous T-cell lymphomas or cutaneous B-cell lymphomas (CBCL), respectively. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is further categorized into 2 types: An indolent form that includes mycosis fungoides, lymphomatoid papulosis, and anaplastic large T-cell primary cutaneous lymphoma An aggressive form that includes Sezary syndrome [4] [5] [6]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The exact cause for mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome has not been established.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Mycosis fungoides tend to affect the older population. Generally, this condition predominately occurs in patients aged older than 50 and is more common in men compared to women, with a ratio of 2:1. The incidence of Sezary syndrome in the United States is about 0.8 to 0.9 cases per million persons per year. Like mycosis fungoides, this condition commonly affects the older adult population and men. The incidence is higher in White populations than Black populations. There is no genetic predisposition and thus no increased risk of developing Sezary syndrome in families of affected patients. [7]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathogenesis of most of the cases of Sezary syndrome is still unknown. However, a small percentage of cases of Sezary syndrome are associated with human T-lymphotropic viruses type 1 and 2 (HTLV-I/II), which are endemic in southern Japan, the Caribbean islands, and part of the Middle East. The typical immunophenotype of the abnormal peripheral T-cell population in Sezary syndrome is clusters of differentiation (CD)3+, CD4+, CD7-, CD26-, CD8-. Occasionally, sezary syndrome can occur when the malignant population demonstrates a CD8+ phenotype or even a CD4-CD8 phenotype. Sezary syndrome with CD8+ phenotype may be associated with HTLV-I/II or HIV. The tumor cells originate from memory T-cells or skin-homing CD4+ T-cells expressing cutaneous lymphocyte antigen (CLA) and chemokine receptors CCR4 and CCR7. Patients with Sezary syndrome have suppressed immunity, as the malignant cells produce type-2 T-cell (Th2) cytokines, which suppress Th1 immunity by decreasing the production of interleukin-12. The role of interleukin-12 is to stimulate the production of interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-a), thus protecting against tumors.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Generally, there are atypical lymphocytes in a sparse dermal infiltrate along with epidermotropism (movement of the atypical lymphocytes into the epidermis), which is suggestive, but not diagnostic, of mycosis fungoides; epidermotropism may be completely absent in biopsies from patients with Sezary syndrome. The more diagnostic intraepidermal aggregates of atypical cells (ie, Pautrier microabscesses) may or may not be present. Significant edema and a nonspecific infiltrate of inflammatory T-cells may predominate, making diagnosis more difficult. [8] Clonality of T-cell receptor gene rearrangement in the skin by polymerase chain reaction is consistent with, but not diagnostic of, mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: The early lesions of mycosis fungoides mimic psoriasis, chronic eczema, atopic dermatitis, leprosy, or lichenoid pityriasis. The typical skin involvement is thin erythematous plaques or flat patches. They present as single or multiple lesions in the gluteal region or thighs. The lesions can be pruritic and remain stable for many years, go into remission, or grow slowly. Sezary syndrome is an erythrodermic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma with a leukemic component. Erythroderma is an intense, widespread, pruritic, exfoliative rash that represents new lesions or progression of prior patches or plaques and is characterized by erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, Sezary or Lutzner cells, atypical circulating lymphocytes, and cutaneous and systemic dissemination of CD4+ T-cells in the blood and the lymph nodes.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: Mycosis fungoides are like a patch or a plaque, whereas Sezary syndrome presents as a diffuse skin rash. The rash involves about 80% of the body's surface area during the disease. Sezary syndrome can be considered a leukemic phase of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma without any bone marrow compromise; involvement of the bone marrow can be seen in advanced disease. The other skin lesions associated with Sezary syndrome include alopecia, keratoderma, hypertrophied nails, lichenification, and ectropion (outward turning of the lower eyelid). Very rarely, it could also involve the visceral organs. Pruritus is intense and can be debilitating; even high doses of antihistamines cannot provide relief. Treatment of underlying cancer with steroids has shown to be effective in controlling pruritus. Due to suppressed immunity, affected people are at higher risk for secondary infections (bacterial and viral) and secondary cancers, including Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Any patient presenting with erythroderma should raise the suspicion of Sezary syndrome. Though the skin involvement is diffuse in Sezary syndrome, it is not as dense as in mycosis fungoides. Therefore, a skin biopsy should be performed without any interventions for the lesions, and the site with the greatest induration should be biopsied. [9] [10] [11]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Excisional lymph node biopsy is preferred, and it can show reactive changes, dermatopathic changes, or features suggestive of lymphoma. Peripheral blood shows atypical circulating lymphocytes with grooved nuclei, called Sezary or Lutzner cells. A rarely smaller variant of Sezary cells can be seen in normal people or those with known malignancy. [12] [13]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Immunophenotyping confirms that T-cell origin (CD3+ and CD4+) and lack of expression of CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7 (mature T-cell antigens) are supportive of Sezary syndrome. The diagnosis is made by erythroderma involving greater than 80% body surface area, clonal T-cell receptor rearrangement confirmed by polymerase chain reaction or Southern blot, and absolute Sezary cell count of at least 1000 cells/μL, or 1 of the following 2 criteria: Increased CD4+ or CD3+ with CD4/CD8 ratio of 10 or more Increased CD4+ cells with abnormal phenotype (CD4+CD7- ratio of 40% or more or CD4+CD26- ratio of 30% or more)

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: The staging of Sezary syndrome and mycosis fungoides involves evaluating the skin (T), lymph nodes (N), visceral organ involvement (M), and blood (B). The types of skin lesions and the extent of their involvement determine the "T" stage. Blood involvement depends on the tumor burden of the blood. Patients with Sezary syndrome are considered to have stages IVA1, IVA2, and IVB, depending on the presence of nodal and visceral involvement.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: The treatment options are based on the stage of the disease. Given the leukemic involvement in Sezary syndrome, the treatment is generally systemic and can be given alone or in combination with skin-based therapy. Patients with stage IVA (no visceral involvement) are usually treated with extracorporeal phototherapy combined with biological response modifiers (retinoids and interferons). Other alternatives include low-dose methotrexate and histone deacetylase inhibitors (vorinostat and romidepsin). Various combinations of the above can be used along with skin-directed therapy.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Skin-directed therapy includes topical or systemic steroids, topical nitrogen mustard, phototherapy (eg, ultraviolet B and psoralen+ultraviolet A), and total skin electron beam therapy.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Radiation therapy can be used for local control of skin and nodal disease.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients with stage IVB (visceral involvement) are usually treated with histone deacetylase inhibitors or targeted therapy like brentuximab vedotin.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Targeted agents approved for mycosis fungoides/Sezary syndrome include brentuximab vedotin (BV) and mogamulizumab. BV is an anti-CD30 monoclonal antibody conjugated with the tubulin inhibitor monomethylauristatin E approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for patients who have received prior therapy; its approval is based on the ALCANZA trial. [14] Moga is a defucosylated humanized antibody directed against the chemokine receptor CCR4 overexpressed on malignant T-cells, and its approval is based on the MAVORIC trial. [15]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: In the relapsed and refractory setting, various single-agent chemotherapies, such as doxorubicin, gemcitabine, and purine/pyrimidine analogs, can be used. FDA-approved drugs in this setting include intermediate-dose methotrexate and pralatrexate. Other options include pembrolizumab, alemtuzumab, bortezomib, and lenalidomide.

content: Young patients with high-risk diseases should be offered allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation at experienced centers.

content: Besides these disease-directed treatment options, pruritis is a strong concern in patients with Sezary syndrome. Various local or systemic options can be used to control pruritis. [16]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Sezary syndrome should be differentiated from mycosis fungoides, psoriasis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, dermatitis, hypereosinophilic syndrome, and adult T-cell leukemia. Primary skin disorders like scabies, drug eruption, and graft-versus-host disease are also in the differential.

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: Skin classification, disease stage, elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels, advanced age, comorbidities, race, male sex, peripheral eosinophilia, large cell transformation, and folliculotropic mycosis fungoides are all factors associated with poor prognosis. These variables have been incorporated into validated prognostic indices, such as the CTCL Severity Index, Cutaneous Lymphoma International Prognostic Index, and Cutaneous Lymphoma International Consortium Prognostic Index. [17]

title: Sezary Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas are best managed by an interprofessional team that includes oncology nurses. Clinicians caring for patients with cutaneous T-cell malignancies should not forget that they improve their quality of life. These patients have severe pruritus, which can be disabling. Thus, the patient should be educated on moisturizing the skin and prescribed medications to relieve the itch. During treatment of the malignancy, the patient's quality of life should be a consideration. The outlook for most patients is guarded.
